test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 29 Dec, 2025 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: The right-hand thumb rule is used to find which of the following?

options.text: Direction of force on a current-carrying conductor
Direction of magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor

solution:
The correct answer is __**Direction of magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Right-hand thumb rule**, often attributed to **Maxwell**, is a fundamental principle in **electromagnetism** used to determine the **direction of magnetic field lines** produced by a **straight current-carrying conductor**.
 
• According to this rule, if a **current-carrying conductor** is held in the **right hand** such that the **thumb points** in the **direction of the electric current**, then the **fingers** will **curl** around the conductor in the **direction of the magnetic field lines**.
 
• This rule visualizes the **magnetic field** as **concentric circles** surrounding the wire. If the **current** flows **upwards**, the **magnetic field** moves in an **anticlockwise direction** (when viewed from above). *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• The **Right-hand thumb rule** does not determine the **magnitude of the current**; the magnitude is usually measured using an **ammeter** in **Amperes (A)**. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*
 
• The **direction of force** on a conductor is determined by **Fleming's Left-Hand Rule**, not the thumb rule. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• The **resistance of a wire** is a property of the material and its dimensions, calculated using **Ohm's Law (V=IR)** or the **resistivity formula**, and is independent of the thumb rule. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Maxwell’s Corkscrew Rule**: 
 
 
• This is another version of the **Right-hand thumb rule**. It states that if a **right-handed corkscrew** is rotated such that it moves in the **direction of the current**, the **direction of rotation** represents the **direction of the magnetic field**.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic Field Properties**:
 
 
• The **strength of the magnetic field** (B) produced by a straight wire is **directly proportional** to the **magnitude of the current** (I) and **inversely proportional** to the **distance** (r) from the wire.
 
• The **S.I. unit** of the **magnetic field** is the **Tesla (T)**.
 
 
 
• **Circular Loops and Solenoids**:
 
 
• The **Right-hand thumb rule** is also applicable to **circular loops**. If the **fingers** curl in the **direction of the current** in the loop, the **thumb points** in the **direction of the magnetic field** at the **center of the loop**.
 
• In a **solenoid**, this rule helps identify the **North and South poles** created by the flow of electricity.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fleming's Left-Hand Rule**: Specifically used for **Electric Motors**. The **thumb** indicates **Motion/Force**, the **forefinger** indicates the **Magnetic Field**, and the **middle finger** indicates the **Current**.
 
• **Fleming's Right-Hand Rule**: Specifically used for **Electric Generators** to find the **direction of induced current**. The **thumb** indicates the **motion of the conductor**, the **forefinger** indicates the **magnetic field**, and the **middle finger** indicates the **induced current**.
 
• **Discovery**: The relationship between **electricity and magnetism** was first observed by **Hans Christian Oersted** in **1820**, when he noticed a **compass needle** deflect near a wire carrying **electric current**.
 
• **Applications**: Understanding these rules is essential for the **design and functioning** of **electromagnets**, **transformers**, **speakers**, and various **industrial sensors**.
